items.question: Fill in each product.

items.title: Nine shares at a two-decimal price
items.question: What does the order cost, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ten shares cost £478.00. Take one share off.

byKey.minus-nine: You took 9 off £478. Nine shares is ten shares less one share, so take off £47.80.
byKey.no-adjust: That is ten shares. One share, £47.80, comes off.
byKey.one-not-lot: You took £1 off. One lot here is a whole share, £47.80.

explain.text: Ten shares cost $10 \times 47.80 = 478.00$ pounds. Nine is one fewer, so $478.00 - 47.80 = 430.20$. The order costs £430.20.

items.title: Two routes to one product
items.prose: Work out $12 \times 96$. You can split 12, or round 96 up to 100.
items.question: What is 12 × 96?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try $12 \times 100$, then take off four lots of 12.

byKey.diagonal: You did $10 \times 90 + 2 \times 6$. That drops two pieces: $10 \times 6$ and $2 \times 90$.
byKey.gap-only: You took off the gap, 4. Each unit of the gap is a lot of 12, so take off 48.
byKey.one-lot: You took off one lot of 12. 96 is four short of 100, so four lots come off.

explain.text: Rounding: $12 \times 100 = 1200$, and four lots of 12 come off: $1200 - 48 = 1152$. Splitting: $10 \times 96 + 2 \times 96 = 960 + 192 = 1152$. Two routes that agree are a free check.

items.title: Scaling a hedge
items.prose: You hold £8,400 of a stock. Its hedge ratio against the index is 0.98, so you sell £0.98 of index for each £1 of stock.
items.question: How much index do you sell, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 0.98 is 0.02 below 1, so take two hundredths of £8,400 off.

byKey.gap-only: You took £2 off. The gap is 0.02 of every pound, so take off 0.02 of £8,400, which is £168.
byKey.one-percent: You took off one hundredth, £84. The gap is two hundredths, so take off £168.
byKey.added: You added 0.02 of it. 0.98 is below 1, so it comes off.

explain.text: $0.98 = 1 - 0.02$, so the hedge is $8400 - 0.02 \times 8400$. A hundredth of £8,400 is £84, so 0.02 of it is £168. You sell £8,232.00 of index.

items.title: A small return on a big book
items.prose: A £4,800,000 book returns 0.0025 of its value today, which is 25 ten-thousandths.
items.question: What is the day's profit, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by 10,000, then multiply by 25.

byKey.two-point-five: That is 0.025 of the book, ten times too big.
byKey.too-small: That is 0.00025 of the book, ten times too small.
byKey.one-percent: That is 100 lots of £480. 25 lots is a quarter of it.
byKey.halved-once: That is 50 lots of £480. Halve again for 25 lots.

explain.text: £4,800,000 ÷ 10,000 = £480. 100 lots of £480 is £48,000, and a quarter is two halvings: £24,000, then £12,000. It is the ×25 move again.

items.title: Why the strips double
items.prose: Show that $(10 + b)^2 = 100 + 20b + b^2$ for any units digit $b$. Each line needs its reason.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $(10 + b)^2 = (10 + b)(10 + b)$, a square is a number times itself
$= 10 \times 10 + 10 \times b + b \times 10 + b \times b$, multiply every part by every part
$= 100 + 20b + b^2$, the two strips are equal, so add them

feedback.correct: Write the square as a product, multiply out, simplify, collect.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by writing the square as a product of two brackets.

byKey.pieces: That line multiplies out two brackets. Write the two brackets first.
byKey.each: Those pieces come from multiplying every part by every part.
byKey.collect: Collecting the strips is the last step.

explain.text: The two middle pieces $10 \times b$ and $b \times 10$ are the two strips of the square. They are equal, so they collect into $20b$. Forgetting one of them is the classic slip: $14^2$ is 196, not 156.

items.title: A square ending in 5
items.prose: Split 85 into 80 and 5, then square it piece by piece.
items.question: What is 85²?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $80^2$, two strips of $80 \times 5$, and $5^2$.

byKey.each-part: You squared 80 and 5 and added. The two strips, 400 each, are missing.
byKey.one-strip: You counted one strip of 400. There are two.
byKey.corner-doubled: You doubled 5 for the corner. It is 5 by 5, so 25.

explain.text: $85^2 = 6400 + 2 \times 400 + 25 = 7225$. Notice $7225$ reads as $8 \times 9 = 72$, then 25. That works for any number ending in 5: $(10n + 5)^2 = 100n(n + 1) + 25$.

items.title: Volatility to variance
items.prose: A fund's annual volatility is 24%, or 0.24. Its variance is the volatility squared.
items.question: What is the variance, as a decimal?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square 24, then give the answer four decimal places.

byKey.point: You have the digits 576, but 0.24 has two decimal places. Its square has four: 0.0576.
byKey.each-part: You squared 0.2 and 0.04 and added. The two strips, 0.008 each, are missing.

explain.text: $24^2 = 400 + 2 \times 80 + 16 = 576$. Since 0.24 has two decimal places, its square has four: $0.0576$.

items.title: One product, three ways
items.prompt: You buy 12 futures contracts at £49.00 each. Work out the cost in your head three ways. First, round 49 to 50 and compensate. Second, split 12 into 10 and 2. Third, use the grid method with both numbers split. Show each working. Then say which way is fastest and why, and name one slip that each method invites.
items.model:
**The cost is £588.00.**

**Compensating.** $49 = 50 - 1$, so twelve lots of 49 is twelve lots of 50, less one lot of 12:

$$12 \times 50 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 = 600$$

$$600 - 12 = 588$$

The payback is one lot of 12, because each contract is £1 under £50.

**Splitting 12.** $12 = 10 + 2$:

$$10 \times 49 + 2 \times 49 = 490 + 98 = 588$$

**Grid method.** $(10 + 2)(40 + 9)$ has four pieces:

$$400 + 90 + 80 + 18 = 588$$

All three agree, so the answer is checked.

**Fastest.** Compensating: one halving and one small subtraction, with no carrying between pieces.

**Slips.** Compensating invites taking off 1 instead of one lot of 12, giving 599. Splitting invites a carrying slip in $490 + 98$, such as 488. The grid invites dropping the two off-diagonal pieces, giving $400 + 18 = 418$.

rubric.text: Compensates correctly: $12 \times 50 = 600$, then takes off one lot of 12, with a reason.
Notes that the three answers agree, as a check.
Picks the fastest method and gives a reason.
Names a real slip for each method, such as 599, a carrying error, or 418.
